10 PERKARA BUKTI ANWAR IBRAHIM TIDAK PANDAI URUS EKONOMI



1. Ramai yang mengatakan DS Anwar Ibrahim (DSAI) adalah seorang yang pandai menguruskan ekonomi ekoran beberapa ucapan beliau sepanjang kempen PRU-15 yang dilihat sering menyentuh isu-isu ekonomi (janji untuk lawan rasuah, bawa pelaburan, selamatkan kewangan kerajaan dan sebagainya). Jom kita telusuri ke alam realiti sejauh mana benarnya apa yang beliau katakan.



2. DSAI pernah memegang beberapa portfolio di dalam Kerajaan Persekutuan. Kementerian yang paling lama dipegang adalah Kementerian Kewangan iaitu daripada tahun 1991 sehingga 1998. Apa yang menjadi perhatian adalah tindakan beliau pada ketika itu dalam menyelesaikan Krisis Kewangan 1997 yang melanda negara. 



3. Beliau terkenal sebagai individu yang sangat mesra dengan pihak Dana Kewangan Antarabangsa (IMF) dan Bank Dunia. Ketika berlakunya krisis tersebut, DSAI menerima cadangan daripada institusi-institusi ini supaya Malaysia mengurangkan perbelanjaan serta menaikkan faedah pinjaman bank dengan tinggi bagi melemahkan ekonomi negara agar mendapat kelayakan untuk menerima bantuan daripada mereka.



4. Sebagai galang gantinya, ekonomi Malaysia mesti diserahkan kepada IMF, seterusnya berpotensi mengakibatkan dasar-dasar yang dibuat seperti Dasar Ekonomi Baru akan dihapuskan. Tindakan ini dikenali sebagai Pakej Penjimatan (Austerity Package), namun seluruh dunia menggelarnya sebagai pengamalan dasar IMF tanpa IMF iaitu tanpa bantuan kewangan yang sepatutnya daripada IMF. 



5. DSAI sempat melaksanakan sebahagian Pakej Penjimatan ini semasa beliau mengambil alih peranan Tun Mahathir sebagai Perdana Menteri secara sementara selama dua bulan. Hasilnya, sebanyak hampir 18% perbelanjaan negara berjaya dipotong dan beberapa projek mega diberhentikan daripada terus beroperasi. 



6. Secara ekonomi, Pakej Penjimatan ketika krisis melanda adalah suatu tindakan berbahaya dan mendapat kritikan hebat daripada pakar-pakar ekonomi di seluruh dunia. Bahkan, menurut kajian yang dibuat oleh tiga orang bekas ahli IMF terhadap 17 negara selama 30 tahun, didapati Pakej Penjimatan ini mengurangkan perbelanjaan penggunaan dan semakin melemahkan ekonomi sesebuah negara. 



7. Sehingga kini, Projek Penjimatan yang dilaksanakan oleh IMF ini menghasilkan kesan yang sangat mendukacitakan dan meletakkan negara yang terlibat dalam krisis yang lebih teruk. Ia bukan sahaja tidak menyelesaikan ekonomi negara tersebut, bahkan meningkatkan jurang kemiskinan (poverty) dan melebarkan ketidaksamaan (inequality) di dalam masyarakat.



8. Akibat tindakan DSAI yang bercanggah dengan perancangan Tun Mahathir dalam menyelesaikan krisis ini, kuasa beliau ke atas kewangan dan ekonomi negara terpaksa dipindahkan kepada Majlis Tindakan Ekonomi Negara (MTEN), sebuah jawatankuasa dan think tank yang ditubuhkan khusus untuk menangani masalah kesusutan nilai Ringgit dan ekonomi negara. 



9. MTEN bertindak melalui pengamalan kawalan matawang (currency control) dan sekatan ke atas CLOB (Central Limit Order Book - pasaran saham haram yang ditubuhkan di Singapura) supaya segala perniagaan Ringgit oleh penyangak matawang seperti Soros dan penjualan saham Malaysia dalam CLOB dapat ditamatkan. 



10. Tindakan MTEN ini berjaya memulihkan ekonomi dan kewangan negara serta kembali ke landasan yang stabil. Tindakan DSAI yang dilihat sangat pro-IMF hampir-hampir meletakkan Malaysia di dalam perangkap hutang IMF buat selama-lamanya seperti berlaku kepada negara-negara lain yang mengambil pendekatan ini.

Menurut logik orang politik yang baru berjinak dengan ilmu Federalisme ni, 

1) Negeri tak boleh ada undang-undang yang macam bertindih dengan pusat.

2) Kalau pusat boleh hukum lebih berat, maka hukuman ringan negeri adalah bodoh dan tak perlu.



Untuk pengetahuan penyokong kerajaan, di negara-negara lain yang amalkan Federalisme, pertindihan antara peraturan pusat dan negeri benda biasa. Kita ambil contoh negara dunia pertama yang asaskan Federalisme iaitu US. Mahkamah pusat dan negeri banyak bertindih, misalnya dalam hukuman terhadap penyalahgunaan dadah dan senjata api haram. 

Contohnya, negeri Virgina haramkan menyimpan barang terkawal iaitu marijuana, methamphetamine, cocaine, dan heroin tapi pusat pula lebih kepada larang pergerakan barang tadi. Kesalahan yang lebih kurang sama dan bertindih antara negeri-negeri dengan pusat tapi hukuman berbeza. Bahkan banyak keadaan, hukuman negeri lebih berat sebab di pusat ada "Sentencing Reform and Correction Act" yang mengurangkan tempoh penjara mandatori untuk jenayah kecil bawah pusat. 

Justeru, bila penyokong kerajaan penuh yakin kata pusat dan negeri tak boleh bertindih, dan hukuman lebih berat lagi bagus, seolah-olah benda ni satu kebenaran mutlak sedunia, orang politik acah-acah pandai ni sebenarnya sebar ajaran sesat.



Satu lagi ajaran sesat penyokong kerajaan ialah menyangka Federalisme bermaksud "negeri wajib mengalah kepada pusat dalam apa jua keadaan", walhal pengasas Federalisme, kata Federalisme ialah kongsi kuasa 50-50 antara pusat dan negeri. Sila baca 85 esei ditulis Alexander Hamilton, James Madison, dan John Jaya pasal konsep persekutuan saja.



Punca kenapa banyak orang salah faham kerana slogan "Bersekutu" di logo negara serta perkataan "Persekutuan" dalam nama Tanah Melayu dan Malaysia. Ini sama macam "Islam ialah agama rasmi persekutuan" yang buat orang salah faham yang Malaysia ni negara Islam, walhal kita negara bersistem sekular. 

Malaysia nampak macam Federalisme sebab ada guna perkataan "persekutuan" dan ada negeri-negeri tetapi sebenarnya kita bukan Federalisme sebenar, kita lebih macam persekutuan Afrika Selatan, cuma baik sikit. Daripada segi amalan sebenar, negara-negara Unitary seperti United Kingdom dan Jepun lebih Federalisme berbanding Malaysia daripada segi keseimbangan antara pusat dengan kawasan. 



Apabila penyokong kerajaan atau penyokong keputusan Nik Elin suruh kita patuh, faham Federalisme, saya tertanya "Adakah mereka ni bengong? Kat celah mana Federalisme nya?" 

Sebab Federalisme ialah ke arah kongsi kuasa 50-50 antara pusat dan negeri, maknanya mesti decentralization atau serah lebih kuasa kepada negeri. 

Kalau ikut kepercayaan penyokong kerajaan dan penyokong kes Nik Elin, kena beri kuasa kepada pusat, itu ialah "Unitary"! 



Kerajaan sebenarnya terbahagi kepada 3 tahap (3-tier) daripada atas ke bawah iaitu:

1) Pusat

2) Negeri / Kawasan

3) Tempatan (PBT)



Di setiap satu tahap kerajaan di atas, ia terbahagi kepada 3 bahagian secara mendatar iaitu:



1) Pelaksana (Eksekutif)

2) Perundangan (Legislatif)

3) Mahkamah.

Setiap bahagian di melintang ni tak boleh campur urusan satu sama lain. 



Di US, setiap bandar (Tahap 3), ada eksekutif, malah ada legislatif dan mahkamah. Legislatif untuk bandar diundi dalam pilihanraya PBT. Di Malaysia, PBT hanya ada pelaksana. 



Di US, negeri-negeri ada eksekutif, mahkamah dan legislatif. Tak seperti Malaysia, negeri US bidang kuasa lebih kurang sama dengan pusat, bezanya mereka tak boleh cetak duit sendiri dan isytihar perang ke negara lain. Itu saja.



Dewan undangan di negeri-negeri US, bukan saja bidang kuasa amat luas tapi struktur berkesan. Sebab ia bicameral.



Di Malaysia, bicameral ni hanya di peringkat pusat sebab ada Dewan Rakyat dan Dewan Negara (2 dewan). Di negeri-negeri US, dewan mereka pun ada 2, malah senator mereka lebih baik daripada Malaysia. Senator Malaysia hampir semuanya dilantik tetapi di negeri-negeri US dan pusat US, senator diundi dalam pilihanraya!



Dewan di negeri-negeri Malaysia adalah Unicameral, ada 1 dewan saja, sama macam dewan untuk PBT di US. 



Semasa Persekutuan Tanah Melayu ditubuhkan pada 1957, bidang kuasa negeri dibataskan kepada undang-undang Islam, tanah, pertanian/hutan, PBT dan perkhidmatan tempatan, jentera negeri. 5 ni saja. Sejak Sabah Sarawak masuk, kuasa negeri-negeri Melayu yang tinggal 5 pun dihakis secara besar-besaran. 



Ini dibuat dengan pusat buat pertindihan fungsi. Misalnya, buat akta parlimen pusat berkaitan berkaitan tanah, hutan dan Islam. Selepas ada akta, pusat tubuhkan agensi atau jabatan pusat berkaitan lalu diberi dana. 



Walaupun perlembagaan mengkhusus 5 bidang tu kepada negeri-negeri, kuasa tu tak dapat dibuat sebab kerajaan guna duit melalui jabatan pusat, tak bagi dana kepada negeri. Negeri bila tiada duit, tidak dapat laksana kuasa.



Negeri-negeri di US boleh pungut cukai pendapatan, sama macam pusat. Di Malaysia, hanya pusat pungut cukai pendapatan dan cukai perbelanjaan. Negeri-negeri Malaysia tak boleh pinjam duit kecuali dari pusat, tapi negeri-negeri boleh pinjam duit dari luar.



Oleh itu, Malaysia bukan lah negara Federalisme lebih-lebih lagi akhir-akhir ni. Kalau penyokong kerajaan atau penyokong kes Nik Elin nak kata kita mesti hormati semangat pusat atau sistem Unitary, itu betul. Tapi kalau kata, penentang kes Nik Elin sebagai tiada semangat persekutuan atau tak faham Federalisme, itu salah.

PETALING JAYA: An academic has urged the government to redefine “national culture” to reflect Malaysia’s diversity and “restore the dignity” of various communities.



Tajuddin Rasdi, an Islamic architecture professor at UCSI University, said a new definition will also help the country “outgrow the past”.



The National Culture Policy (NCP), formulated at the 1971 National Culture Congress, outlines three conditions to define a “Malaysian culture”, namely that it must be based on Malay culture, suitable elements from other cultures may be accepted, and Islam is an important component.



Tajuddin recalled that not many non-Malays were present at the congress, which came after the May 13, 1969 riots, but there was a strong Malay presence.



“I think that was where we started and I have no issue with it because this is history. History arises from a reaction towards a certain situation,” he told FMT.



“But I do believe that we need to outgrow the past. The new generation needs the dignity of their own identities, and therefore the current definition must be reviewed. We should have an equal statement for all cultures,” he added.



The NCP has never been gazetted into law but it is said to have contributed to tense racial relationships.



It has often been invoked to deny the recognition of non-Malay cultures, such as the ban on lion dances and other non-Malay cultural forms in schools in the 1980s.



A 2022 Unesco report has rated Malaysia as one of the countries with the lowest inter-cultural dialogue index (ICDI), giving it a score of 0.35 out of one.



Tajuddin said the intensification of Islamic thought during the Islamic reform movements in the 1970s and the growth of a retiring Malay middle-class that has become more religious would account for the low score.



“Islam has become bigger and bigger, and it engulfs the idea of culture. I’m not saying that it is right or wrong. I’m saying that this is how the Muslims and the Malays react to (the idea of culture),” he said.



“There’s hardly anything you can call Malay culture (now) unless it is associated with Islam. One reason why there is a lack of cultural dialogue between Malays and others is simply because of this,” he added.



Some Malay arts, such as wayang kulit and mak yong, have also been deemed “un-Islamic” by religious authorities, he said.



Tajuddin added that the current political landscape has also exacerbated the lack of communication between the Muslim and non-Muslim communities as religion has become a “selling point” in politics.



The solution, he said, lies in educating the Muslim clerics on topics of arts, culture and discourses in other civilisations, as they wield great influence on public opinion.



“Islam is supposed to be able to coexist with Chinese and Indian cultures but there are certain things that you might have to modify. It doesn’t mean engulfing others’ (cultures).



“If you can retrain clerics who write sermons by teaching them art, culture and world civilisation, we can then eradicate racial politics because Islam is not supposed to be racist,” he added.



Unesco’s index doesn’t reflect Malaysia’s diversity 



Eddin Khoo, who is patron of the cultural organisation Pusaka, said the ICDI does not necessarily reflect the actual diversity experienced by Malaysians on a daily basis.



“Inter-cultural dialogue is happening every day in the lives of Malaysians. There are more inter-cultural marriages now than before,” he said.



“As for formalised inter-cultural dialogues, it’s not that they are not happening, it’s just that they are ineffective,” he added.



Citing Pusaka’s efforts in advocating local performances with roots in other cultures, such as Teochew puppetry, Urumee Melum and Reog Ponogoro, Khoo said Malaysians should understand that the nation belongs to a “highly syncretic diasporic culture”.



“Malaysia is a place where everything can ‘fall and settle’. Why have we forgotten that? Stop pretending or subscribing to the idea of (cultural) puritanism that has never existed (here) in the first place,” Khoo added.

Islam, Beyond Reform



With every terror attack, clamour for reform in Islam goes up as a crisis is alleged in the religion. The same happened after the beheadings in France in response to Prophet Muhammad’s cartoons. People say that since Islam has remained unreformed, its anachronistic understanding has been at the root of much of the bad publicity that its more zealous followers have been inviting to it.

Verses from the Quran are quoted to both arraign and absolve Islam. Defences are mounted arguing whether these are to be understood literally or metaphorically, and to be seen in their contextual terms or transcendental claims. Since much of the contestations centre around the meanings of the canonical literature, the Quran and the Hadith, it is hoped that if these were given a contemporaneous interpretation, Islam would become more compatible with the modern world, and it would cease to yield justifications for regressive practices and violent actions.



This optimism tends to forget that religions don’t change much, and that the words of scriptures can’t be erased and overwritten. Neither the verses can be changed, nor their conventional understanding. As for the interpretation, there is a limit to the point it can be stretched into yielding allegorical or contextual meanings. In any case, believers don’t have any problem with either the text or its age-old meaning. They try to mould their world in accordance with the precepts of the religion. To them, stretching the meaning to measure up to the present world may amount to a subversive reversal of order.

Calls for Reformation in Islam are fashionable, but miss a crucial point.



Islam needs ‘relocation’

The reform, if any, has to be in one’s attitude towards the religion, and not in how Islam is interpreted, understood and practiced. The shift in focus from the transcendent to mundane, divine to human, and religious to secular has to be the basis of reform. If people continue to depend on religion for inspiration and justification for their actions, and they don’t graduate to the higher morality of secularism and modernity, no matter how they reinterpret their religion, they would continue to regress. In any case, when it comes to religion, the orthodox position, being of classical vintage, commands better legitimacy.



Therefore, rather than reformation of Islam, its relocation and reformulation may be a better ideal. Like other religions in the modern age, Islam too should be relocated to where religions belong — the private sphere. The longer any religion remains part of the public sphere, higher the chances of its politicisation and radicalisation.



Religion, after all, is a way of worship. To say that one’s religion is a way of life is a statement with little meaning. A way of life is the culture, of which, religion is a constituent. However, little would change if the selfish motive of personal salvation continued to disregard the public welfare. Therefore, Islam has to be reformulated as a people friendly and welfare oriented religion that inspires its followers to do good to people here and now, rather than securing paradise for them after death. Such a secularisation would make people humane rather than dogmatic, and compassionate rather than fanatic.



It’s alright to say that the trajectory of European history can’t be the universal template for other societies, but if we were to learn from it, successive stages from renaissance’s humanism to religious reformation to enlightenment to the rise of liberal, secular and democratic world, would have many lessons for us. One of these could be that even the reformed religion was not good enough for the imperatives of the modern world, and it had to be sequestered to the private space in order to let reason have an unfettered movement which, in turn, would enable the rise of higher secular morality.



The Muslims were impelled into both reform and revival by the same impetus — the shock caused by the loss of political ascendancy. Both the trends had the same purpose — restoration of the lost glory. This could be one reason why reform gave way to revivalism so easily, and almost all the late 19th century reform movements from Sir Syed Ahmad Khan’s in India to Muhammad Abduh’s and Rashid Rida’s in Egypt petered out, making way for the militant Islamism.



The unquestioned equation of religion with law, its origins

Unlike Christianity, Islam didn’t have to suffer prolonged persecution. It progressed from acquiring a chieftainship to a State to an empire with lightning rapidity, which turned it into a statist ideology. The religion-cum-ideology was further elaborated into the legal structure of the empire. This led to the unquestioned equation of religion with shariat, and of shariat with law. Therefore, any reform in Islam had to come through the legal route. Accordingly, a long forgotten tool called Ijtihad was brought into re-circulation. This terminology (coming from the same route as jihad) connotes intellectual exertion for deriving a religious ruling in such cases as the Quran and the Hadith are silent about. In contemporary Islamic discourses, Ijtihad is looked up as a noble ideal, but, for obvious reasons, there has been no substantial effort towards its realisation. Most of the Muslim States — from Indonesia, Malaysia, Bangladesh, Pakistan and Turkey in Asia to Egypt, Morocco and Tunisia in Africa — having adopted the modern legal system, pious platitudes notwithstanding, are not going back to the archaic shariah laws. And those which do — the likes of ISIS or Taliban — have no use for Ijtihad.



No wonder that the modern and scientific reinterpretation of Islam has not moved an inch beyond where Sir Syed Ahmad Khan (1817-98) left it. Even though it may be possible, it’s going to be a fruitless exercise and, therefore, undesirable for both the modern and the orthodox Muslims.

The poet Allama Iqbal’s biggest contribution, if his leads were followed, could be the prominence he gave to the word ‘Reconstruction’ in the title of his collection of essays published in 1930, The Reconstruction of Religious Thought in Islam. This word underscored the dilapidation of religious thought in Islam. A lesser man couldn’t get away with such candour. But the orthodoxy was so mesmerised by Iqbal’s stature and erudition that the import of this proposition was lost on their not too acute perception. Be that as it may, nearly a century later, despite his iconic status, his proposed ‘reconstruction’ remains a pipe dream. The reason is same as in the case of Sir Syed. It will be a pointless exercise. The zeitgeist demands not the reformation but the relocation and reformulation; in fact, a veritable transcendence of religion.

Why are so many Malays confused in their own religion?



We often find ourselves caught between conflicting visions of what it means to be a Muslim. Much of this confusion can be traced back to the profound impact of colonialism and orientalism on our understanding of Islam.



Renowned Malaysian scholar Syed Muhammad Naquib al-Attas has deeply analyzed this crisis of Muslim identity. In his seminal work "Islam and Secularism," al-Attas argues that the secular Western worldview, imposed through colonialism, has led to a "deislamization" of Muslim thought and institutions.



Under colonial rule, our traditional Islamic educational system was dismantled and replaced by a Western secular model. This disrupted the transmission of authentic Islamic knowledge and created a false dichotomy between "religious" and "modern" learning that persists to this day.



Moreover, orientalist scholars, while claiming to objectively study Islam, in fact served to construct and promote a version of Islam that fit Western prejudices. They depicted Islam as irrational, backwards, and in need of "reform" along Western lines.



This orientalist vision has been internalized by some Muslim elites and movements, leading to misguided attempts to "modernize" Islam by uncritically adopting Western norms. At the same time, it has fueled a reactive turn to rigid, literalist interpretations of Islam such as wahhabism, that reject the intellectual legacy of Islamic civilization.



The way forward, as al-Attas and other scholars have argued, is a critical revival of authentic Islamic thought and institutions. We must rediscover the depth and breadth of our own tradition, engaging with the works of great Muslim thinkers and the diverse heritage of Islamic civilizations.



This involves a "dewesternization" of Islamic thought, as al-Attas puts it - not a rejection of all things Western, but a critical engagement with Western ideas from a firmly rooted Islamic perspective. It also means reviving and reforming our institutions of Islamic learning, so that they can produce scholars and leaders grounded in authentic Islamic knowledge while being equipped to address contemporary challenges.



Only by reclaiming our Islamic intellectual heritage and confidently articulating our own vision of Islam can we as Malaysian Muslims overcome the crisis of identity that is the legacy of colonialism. It is a daunting task, but one we must undertake for the future of our ummah.

Sisters in Islam (SIS) is appalled by the latest news in Terengganu where six individuals were arrested, imprisoned and summoned by the Jabatan Hal Ehwal Agama Terengganu (JHEAT) for deliberately missing their Friday prayers.

Article 11 in the Malaysia Constitution states that everyone is free to practice their religion. It is therefore unbecoming to see religious bodies like JHEAT failing to uphold these basic values.



This act of moral policing by JHEAT violates the basic tenets of Islam which stand for justice, compassion and peace. The Quran clearly states that no one should be forced into practicing any religion in its verse, “Let there be no compulsion in religion” [2:256]. 



“Moral policing” in the name of Islam is a cruel way of showing abuse of power which needs to be addressed and banished. There are many verses in the Quran that rejects this act of spying and backbiting such as, “do not spy on each other behind their backs” [49:12], “do not enter other houses except yours without first asking permission; and if asked to go away, turn back for this is proper for you” [24:27-28] and “when you judge among the people, do so equitably” [4:58]. It was also reported that our Prophet said, “do not go out and search for the fault of others” (Sunan Al Dawood, 2283).



JHEAT’s disgraceful act of spying shows an act of misplaced priorities for the country as there are many other pressing issues that need to be addressed more urgently such as poverty, child marriage, female genital mutilation, domestic violence, marital rape and others.



We call for the immediate release of the men who have been charged and for laws to be reformed from being punitive to reformative, in line with the spirit of Rahmatan lil Alamin as promoted by Datuk Seri Mujahid Yusof Rawa. Initiatives should instead be put in place to promote greater understanding of Islam as a gentle religion whose followers are compelled to practice willingly out of love for God, instead of out of fear for man.

16 Januari 2025 (Khamis) | UniSZA Kampus Gong Badak

 

Fakulti Perniagaan dan Pengurusan (FPP), UniSZA dengan kerjasama Terengganu Incorporated Sdn Bhd telah menganjurkan Professorial Talk 3.0 yang bertajuk ‘Islamic Finance: Driving Value-Based Industry Reform for Sustainable Solutions’ dan telah dihadiri lebih 200 orang peserta daripada kalangan ahli korporat dan akademik yang berlangsung di Dewan Perdana, UniSZA Kampus Gong Badak.



Program bual bicara ini telah dikendalikan oleh Prof. Madya Dr. Muhammad Shahrul Ifwat bin Ishak, Pengarah Islamic Social Finance Centre, UniSZA yang turut menampilkan penceramah jemputan: Prof. Dr. Engku Rabiah Adawiyah binti Engku Ali yang merupakan Honorary Professor di Institute of Islamic Banking and Finance, UIAM dan mempunyai kepakaran dalam bidang Kewangan Islam, Takaful, Tadbir Urus Korporat dan Pelaburan Islam dan juga Encik Mohd Zikri bin Mohd Shairy yang merupakan Director, Social Finance di Bank Islam Malaysia Berhad dan telah berkecimpung dalam industri kewangan Islam selama 18 tahun serta mempunyai pengalaman yang luas dalam tadbir urus syariah bank Islam terutamanya nasihat syariah dan pengurusan risiko syariah.



Perasmian program ini telah disempurnakan oleh YBrs. Encik Burhanuddin Hilmi bin Mohamed @ Harun, Presiden dan Ketua Pegawai Eksekutif Kumpulan, Terengganu Incorporated Sdn Bhd yang turut disertai oleh YBrs. Prof. Dr. Zuhairah Ariff binti Abd Ghadas, Timbalan Naib Canselor (Akademik dan Antarabangsa) selaku wakil Naib Canselor UniSZA. Beliau menekankan bahawa komitmen syarikat bukan sahaja mengukuhkan kesihatan kewangannya tetapi juga memainkan peranan penting dalam menggalakkan pembangunan ekonomi yang mampan dan beretika. Pendekatan ini mengukuhkan prinsip teras keadilan, ketelusan dan tanggungjawab sosial, memastikan amalan kewangan menyumbang secara positif kepada pertumbuhan jangka panjang rantau ini.



Turut hadir pada majlis tersebut ialah YBrs. Prof. Madya Dr. Mazuri binti Abd. Ghani, Dekan Fakulti Perniagaan dan Pengurusan, UniSZA serta barisan Pengurusan Eksekutif Fakulti Perniagaan dan Pengurusan, UniSZA dan juga barisan Pengurusan Terengganu Incorporated Sdn Bhd.



UniSZA menaruh harapan tinggi agar program ini dapat menyebarkan kesedaran tentang pelaburan Islam dan pentingnya mematuhi prinsip syariah dalam aktiviti kewangan.
